ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: As shown in the figure, in the right-angled triangle ABC, $\angle ACB=90^\circ$, $AB=7$, the point D is the midpoint of $AB$, the point P is a moving point on the hypotenuse $AB$, $FG$ is the perpendicular bisector of the line segment $CP$, Q is a moving point on $FG$. What is the minimum value of $PQ+QD$?
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text:
\textbf{Solution:} Let's connect $CQ$, $CD$ as shown in the figure,\\
since point P is a moving point on the hypotenuse $AB$, $FG$ is the perpendicular bisector of the line segment $CP$, Q is a moving point on $FG$,\\
therefore $CQ=PQ$,\\
thus $PQ+QD=CQ+DQ\ge CD$,\\
since $\angle ACB=90^\circ$, $AB=7$, and point D is the midpoint of $AB$,\\
therefore $CD=\frac{7}{2}$.\\
Hence, the minimum value of $PQ+QD$ is $\boxed{\frac{7}{2}}$.

raw_record.original_question: As shown in the figure, in the right-angled triangle ABC, $\angle ACB=90^\circ$, $AB=7$, the point D is the midpoint of $AB$, the point P is a moving point on the hypotenuse $AB$, $FG$ is the perpendicular bisector of the line segment $CP$, Q is a moving point on $FG$. What is the minimum value of $PQ+QD$?
raw_record.answer: \textbf{Solution:} Let's connect $CQ$, $CD$ as shown in the figure, since point P is a moving point on the hypotenuse $AB$, $FG$ is the perpendicular bisector of the line segment $CP$, Q is a moving point on $FG$, therefore $CQ=PQ$, thus $PQ+QD=CQ+DQ\ge CD$, since $\angle ACB=90^\circ$, $AB=7$, and point D is the midpoint of $AB$, therefore $CD=\frac{7}{2}$. Hence, the minimum value of $PQ+QD$ is $\boxed{\frac{7}{2}}$.
raw_record.final_cot: Image description: The figure is triangle ABC, A and B are at the two ends of the base AB, C is above, and there is a right-angle mark at C, so AB is the hypotenuse; P and D are both marked on AB; an oblique line FG passes through the figure, and point Q is on FG; the figure also draws the segments from P to C, from P to Q, and from D to Q. Reasoning: The problem statement gives that FG is the perpendicular bisector of segment CP, and Q is on FG, therefore the distances from Q to C and P are equal, namely PQ=CQ. So PQ+QD=CQ+QD. For triangle CQD, use the triangle inequality, giving CQ+QD≥CD, therefore PQ+QD≥CD. Also because △ABC is right-angled at C, and D is the midpoint of hypotenuse AB, the midpoint of the hypotenuse is equidistant from the three vertices, so CD=AB/2=7/2. Thus PQ+QD≥7/2. This lower bound can be reached: take P=A or P=B, and take Q=D; at this time D is equidistant from C and P, and D lies on the perpendicular bisector of CP, so PQ+QD=7/2. Therefore the minimum value is 7/2.
